chunks: How a digital oscilloscope works. The question: How does an oscilloscope work?
A digital scope scales the input signal to a usable size, measures it very quickly with a converter (an ADC), and stores the numbers in memory.
A trigger circuit watches the signal and decides which moment counts as "time zero". A processor then connects the stored points into a smooth trace and draws it.
Each stage has its own limit on what you can see.
Think of a security camera that records on a loop and keeps only the last few minutes. When an alarm trips, it saves what happened just before and just after, then stops.
A scope does the same. Its converter writes samples into a memory that keeps overwriting the oldest ones.
When the trigger fires, the scope keeps recording for a bit, then freezes. That is how it can show the moments before an event.
The signal runs top to bottom through conditioning, ADC and memory to the display. The trigger takes a branch off the amplifier output and tells the memory when to stop writing.
The timebase clock drives both the ADC and the trigger timing.
ADC: a converter that turns a voltage into a number. Sample rate: how many measurements per second the ADC takes. Memory depth: how many samples the scope can hold in one capture.
Trigger: a circuit that fires when the signal crosses a chosen level, marking time zero. Bandwidth: the fastest signal the input stage can pass before it rounds the signal off.
Suppose a scope has 10 million points of memory and samples at 1 billion samples per second. It holds 10 to the 7 over 10 to the 9 equals 0.

So the scope spreads the samples out to 10 million per second. That is one sample every 100 nanoseconds.
A 20 nanoseconds glitch could fall between two samples and never be recorded. That is the whole idea.
"A digital scope conditions the input with coupling, an attenuator and an amplifier, then a fast ADC samples it into a circular memory.
A separate trigger comparator decides which moment is time zero, so the scope can stop after enough post-trigger samples and show the history before it too.
The processor interpolates, decimates and draws the waveform. So bandwidth, sample rate, ADC bits and memory depth each limit the picture in their own way."
